title: Billionaires, Foundations, and the Giving Pledge
text:
Data Story  ·  Giving Pledge · Candid · UBS/Forbes  ·  2010–2025

In 2010, Bill Gates, Melinda French Gates, and Warren Buffett launched the Giving Pledge, asking the world’s wealthiest people to commit at least half their fortunes to charity. Fifteen years on, the number of billionaires has nearly tripled and the number of private foundations has more than doubled — but the Giving Pledge itself has lost momentum, with new sign-ups slowing to a trickle even as the fortunes it was designed to redirect keep growing.






1 — The Giving Pledge: Cumulative Signatories

  The pledge grew quickly in its first decade, then stalled. Just 4 new signatories joined
  in 2024 — a record low — before a modest rebound to 14 in 2025. Today the pledge counts
  256 signatories from roughly 30 countries, of whom about 110 are US billionaires —
  roughly 12% of America's billionaire population.


  


  Cumulative signatories to the Giving Pledge by year. Compiled from the Giving Pledge
  public signatory list, the Institute for Policy Studies report "The Giving Pledge at 15"
  (2025), and contemporaneous press coverage. Figures for individual years are
  approximate, interpolated between known totals.



2 — Number of US Private Foundations

  While headline philanthropy debates focus on a handful of billionaire names, the
  private foundation sector has quietly more than doubled in size since 2010 — from
  roughly 70,000 to over 150,000 registered foundations, most of them small family
  foundations rather than the mega-funds that dominate the news.


  


  Number of private foundations registered in the United States. 2011 and 2015 figures
  from the Foundation Center; 2023–2025 figures from Candid. Intermediate years are
  estimated via smoothed interpolation.



3 — Number of Billionaires Worldwide

  The billionaire population has grown in step with — and arguably faster than — both
  the foundation sector and the Giving Pledge. Global billionaire wealth has surged 81%
  since 2020 alone, reaching an estimated $18.3 trillion in 2025.


  


  Number of individuals with net worth over $1 billion, worldwide. Source: Forbes
  World's Billionaires List (annual), with 2025 figure corroborated by UBS Billionaire
  Ambitions Report. Counts vary slightly by methodology and snapshot date.



4 — Relative Growth, Indexed to 2010

  Putting all three series on the same scale (2010 = 100) shows the real story: the
  Giving Pledge kept pace with billionaire growth for its first decade, but new sign-ups
  have nearly dried up since 2023 even as billionaire wealth and the foundation sector
  continue to expand.


  


  All three series indexed to 100 at 2010. This normalization shows relative growth
  rates rather than absolute scale — the underlying populations differ by several
  orders of magnitude (hundreds of signatories vs. thousands of billionaires vs.
  hundreds of thousands of foundations).




  
    Giving Pledge signatories, 2025
    256
    From ~30 countries; ~110 are US billionaires (~12% of US billionaire population)
  
  
    New sign-ups, 2024
    4
    Record low — down from 113 in the pledge's first five years (2010–2015)
  
  
    US private foundations, 2025
    151,000+
    More than double the 2011 count of 73,764
  
  
    Global billionaires, 2025
    2,891
    Up 58% from 1,826 in 2015; combined wealth ~$18.3 trillion (+81% since 2020)

title: Boston’s Windiest Year: What the Record Actually Shows

title: Boston’s Windiest Year: What the Record Actually Shows
section: A deliberately partial picture
text:
A deliberately partial picture
This post is narrower in scope than the temperature posts on this site, and it’s worth saying why up front. Boston’s annual average high and low temperatures are compiled year-by-year in public, ready-to-use datasets going back to the 1890s. Wind is not treated the same way: the underlying daily and annual wind measurements exist in NOAA’s archives, but nobody has published the full year-by-year average wind speed series in a form that’s readily accessible without a direct bulk download from NOAA’s climate data systems.
What follows, then, is built entirely from specific, documented reference points — individual facts reported by NOAA/NCEI, the Iowa Environmental Mesonet, and the Boston Globe’s weather coverage — rather than a reconstructed year-by-year time series. Where a number below is a single documented data point rather than part of a continuous series, that’s noted explicitly. A fuller post, with an actual annual series, is a natural thing to come back to if a direct route to NOAA’s underlying station data opens up.




Record begins 1936 Continuous wind observations at Logan Airport — 89 years of record as of 2025


2025 average wind gust 30.6 mph The windiest year on record at Logan since 1936


Long-term average wind gust ~23 mph 2025 finished roughly 8 mph above this historical norm


Days with gusts ≥ 60 mph, 2025 5 A new record, surpassing the previous mark of 4 such days (set in 1977, 2011, and 2012)

title: Boston’s Windiest Year: What the Record Actually Shows
section: Gusts up, sustained wind more ambiguous
text:
Gusts up, sustained wind more ambiguous
Gusts and sustained wind speed are genuinely different measurements, not just two ways of describing the same thing. Sustained wind speed is the average flow over a two-minute stretch; a gust is a brief, sharp spike that can last a few seconds to half a minute. Boston’s 2025 story is really a story about gusts specifically: through the first half of 2025, gusts were averaging nearly 32.6 mph, more than 2 mph above the previous record pace set in 2010, and Logan recorded gusts of 30 mph or higher on 165 days that year — roughly two and a half times the yearly average for days that gusty.
Sustained wind speed tells a more ambiguous story. Through the first half of 2025, sustained wind speed averaged 12.28 mph — the highest since 2000, and above the trailing 30-year average — but still below the full 89-year average for the station. Taken at face value, that means Logan’s sustained winds have historically run higher, on average, over the full 20th-century record than they have in the more recent 30-year normal period, even as 2025’s gusts were setting all-time records. That’s a genuinely interesting tension worth investigating further, but it isn’t one this post can fully resolve without the complete annual series in hand.

title: Boston’s Windiest Year: What the Record Actually Shows
section: Why Boston is windy at all
text:
Why Boston is windy at all
Boston’s wind isn’t a fluke of any one year. Among major U.S. cities, Boston is the single windiest, with average wind speeds about 2 mph higher than second-place Chicago (the city that actually carries the “Windy City” nickname) and roughly twice the average wind speed of Phoenix, the calmest major U.S. city. The explanation researchers point to is location: Logan sits on the coast, close to the North Atlantic’s active storm track, which is also why a warming ocean and atmosphere can plausibly push the upper end of storm intensity higher without necessarily changing the day-to-day average by much — a distinction that may help explain why 2025 broke gust records so clearly while its sustained-wind story stayed more mixed.


Sources: National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) and Iowa Environmental Mesonet wind data for Boston Logan International Airport (GHCND:USW00014739), as reported in Boston Globe coverage (“So far, 2025 has been the windiest year on record for Boston, statistics show,” June 2025; “Boston, windy? The city clocked 100 more blustery days than usual, making 2025 the windiest yet,” January 2026); Current Results, “Windiest City in America,” based on NOAA National Climatic Data Center Comparative Climatic Data.

title: The Rest of What the Smartphone Killed
section: Four graveyards, four different data sources
text:
Four graveyards, four different data sources
Putting these on one chart means stitching together four industries that don’t track themselves the same way. Digital camera shipments are CIPA’s, the same series used in the earlier post on this site. Smartphone shipments are IDC’s, as in the BlackBerry post. Portable GPS (personal navigation device, or PND) shipments come from a mix of Statista’s tracked series and Garmin’s own SEC filings — Garmin was around 30–38% of the global PND market through this period, so its filings are a useful cross-check even though the chart uses total-market figures, not Garmin alone. iPod unit sales are Apple’s own reported figures, by fiscal year (Apple’s fiscal year runs October–September, close enough to calendar year not to distort the shape of the curve). Camcorders don’t have a clean global aggregate at all — CIPA and IDC don’t track them, so that category gets a separate case study below instead of a line on the chart.
The PND and iPod series both stop partway through the chart, and that’s deliberate rather than a data gap: both categories didn’t decline to some small stable niche the way cameras did. They mostly stopped being tracked as distinct products, because they stopped being distinct products — Garmin pivoted its PND-era engineering into fitness watches and marine/aviation electronics, and Apple folded the iPod Touch into being basically a Wi-Fi-only iPhone until discontinuing the whole line in 2022.








Worldwide unit shipments, log scale. Cameras: CIPA (all types combined). Smartphones: IDC (2007–2009 estimated). Portable GPS: Statista-tracked global PND shipments and Garmin SEC filings, 2007–2015 only — the mass-market auto-PND category effectively stopped being tracked as a distinct global aggregate after that. iPod: Apple’s own reported unit sales by fiscal year, 2007–2014 only — the last year Apple broke the category out separately.

title: The Rest of What the Smartphone Killed
section: The one that doesn’t fit on the chart: camcorders
text:
The one that doesn’t fit on the chart: camcorders
The Flip Video camera is worth a stat card of its own because its rise-and-fall happened almost entirely within the smartphone-camera era, compressed into five years rather than a decade. Pure Digital Technologies launched the Flip in 2006 as a stripped-down, pocket-sized camcorder that did one thing well: record decent video and get it onto a computer with a flip-out USB connector, no cables required. It sold nearly 5 million units by September 2010 and briefly became the #1-selling camcorder brand in the US. Cisco, which had bought the brand for $590 million in 2009, killed it in April 2011 — one day before a new model was due on shelves. The reasoning was almost apologetic: smartphone video had gotten good enough, and more importantly, uploadable enough, that a device whose entire pitch was “simple to shoot, simple to share” had nothing left to be simple about.


Flip camcorder lifespan 2006–2011 Five years from launch to discontinuation, most of it spent as the US’s #1 camcorder brand


Units sold before shutdown ~5M Cumulative worldwide sales through September 2010, per Cisco’s own figures

title: The Rest of What the Smartphone Killed
section: The feature that made all of this permanent: sharing
text:
The feature that made all of this permanent: sharing
Every product on that chart lost a hardware race, but the deeper thing they lost was a distribution race. A camera, a GPS unit, or an MP3 player was a closed loop — whatever it captured or calculated stayed on the device until you plugged it into a computer. What made the smartphone different wasn’t just that it combined those features; it’s that whatever it captured could be online, in front of other people, in seconds. That only mattered because, starting almost exactly when the iPhone did, hundreds of millions of people suddenly had somewhere to put it.





Monthly active users (or the closest comparable figure — see note). Facebook and Instagram figures are the companies’ own disclosed milestones (SEC filings and press releases), interpolated between announced numbers where a platform didn’t report every year. MySpace figures are far less reliable: the company reported registered accounts, unique monthly visitors, and “active users” inconsistently and sometimes simultaneously (contemporary press cited anywhere from 76 million to over 200 million for the same period); the line here uses the comScore-style monthly-unique-visitor estimates most comparable to how Facebook counted MAUs, and should be read as order-of-magnitude, not exact. Friendster’s numbers are even messier — heavily front-loaded with now-inactive accounts and later dominated by a pivot to Southeast Asia — and aren’t charted for that reason.



MySpace peak, 2008 ~76M Monthly unique visitors — the same year Facebook’s own user base passed 100 million and never looked back


Facebook, 2007 → 2012 58M → 1.06B Crossed a billion monthly active users five years after MySpace’s peak


Instagram to 100M users ~28 months Launched Oct. 2010, mobile-only from day one, acquired by Facebook at 30M users in 2012


Facebook photo uploads, 2007 14M/day Already the web’s largest photo-sharing service before Instagram existed, per comScore

title: The Rest of What the Smartphone Killed
section: Back to BlackBerry, one more time
text:
Back to BlackBerry, one more time
This is the piece that makes the BlackBerry story make sense as more than a punchline. BlackBerry added a camera in 2006, a full two years before Instagram existed and before Facebook had cracked 100 million users — the camera was, for a while, ahead of anywhere good to put the photos. By the time Instagram launched in October 2010, BlackBerry’s own App World was over a year old, chronically thin on quality apps, and its browser couldn’t render most of the mobile web properly. RIM had the hardware pattern right in 2006 and the distribution pattern wrong for the rest of the decade — which, across every device on the chart above, turns out to be the difference that mattered.

Sources: Camera & Imaging Products Association (CIPA); International Data Corporation (IDC) Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker; Garmin Ltd. SEC filings (Forms 8-K) and Statista’s tracked global PND shipment series; Apple Inc. fiscal-year unit sales disclosures; Cisco Systems and contemporaneous press coverage (PetaPixel, SlashGear, CBC) on the Flip Video camcorder; Facebook/Meta SEC filings (Form 10-K) and press disclosures; Instagram/Meta press disclosures; MySpace user figures as reported by Hootsuite, comScore-derived estimates, and contemporaneous press (Forbes, CBS News, Strixus) — flagged above as the least reliable series on this page.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis
text: Machine Learning for Social Science  ·  Boston, MA

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis
section: Abstract
text:
Abstract
Design. Observational, correlational study combining a cross-sectional comparison across countries with a longitudinal time series within a single country. Objective. To estimate the Pearson correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita (i) across 175 countries at one point in time (2023–2024) and (ii) within the United States annually from 1960 to 2024, and to compare the two. Methods. Publicly available national statistics; Pearson correlation coefficients computed on both untransformed and log-transformed income. Results. Both designs show a strong positive association: r = 0.86 (log income) in the cross-section (n = 175, p < 10−50) and r = 0.97 (log income) in the US time series (n = 65, p < 10−39). Conclusion. The correlation is strong and positive under both designs, but a correlation coefficient alone cannot distinguish a direct effect of income from a shared trend or common cause — a limitation addressed further in the discussion.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis
section: Introduction
text:
Introduction

Background and rationale
The association between national income and population health is one of the best-documented empirical regularities in economic demography, generally credited to Samuel Preston’s 1975 cross-national comparison of life expectancy and GDP per capita (the “Preston curve”). The relationship is concave: a given increase in income buys much more life expectancy in a poor country than in a rich one. It is also, definitionally, a cross-sectional finding — different countries compared at a single point in time.
A separate and logically independent question is whether the same association holds within a country as it develops over time. This distinction matters because a relationship that is real and strong in a cross-section need not describe what happens to any single unit as it moves through time — a problem long recognized in the social sciences as the ecological fallacy (Robinson, 1950) and, in this specific empirical setting, documented directly by Preston himself: national time series of income growth explain only a modest share of a country’s own gains in life expectancy over the twentieth century, with the cross-sectional curve itself shifting upward decade by decade. This series has now checked that same cross-section/time-series distinction for three different pairs of variables (women’s labor force participation and income; urbanization and income; and here, life expectancy and income), because it is a general methodological question, not one specific to any variable pair.


Objectives

To estimate the Pearson correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita across countries at one point in time (a cross-sectional design).
To estimate the Pearson correlation between the same two variables within a single country (the United States) across a 65-year period (a time-series design).
To compare the two estimates and consider what a simple correlation coefficient can, and cannot, establish about the relationship in each design.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis
section: Methods
text:
Methods

Study design
Two designs are reported side by side: (i) a cross-sectional design, in which each country contributes a single observation at approximately the same point in time; and (ii) a time-series design, in which a single country (the United States) contributes one observation per year over 65 consecutive years. No intervention, treatment assignment, or manipulation of any kind was involved in either design; both are purely observational.


Setting
The cross-sectional design covers all countries for which both variables were available in the sources described below, observed in the most recent year each source publishes (GDP per capita: 2023; life expectancy: most recent CIA World Factbook estimate, referenced 2024). The time-series design covers the United States, annually, from 1960 (the first year both source series report) to 2024.


Participants (units of analysis)
Cross-section: All sovereign states and territories for which a numeric value was available for both life expectancy and GDP per capita in the sources below, matched by country name (with manual reconciliation of naming differences, e.g., “South Korea” vs. “Korea, Rep.”). Of 229 countries and territories with a life expectancy figure, 175 (76%) had a matching GDP per capita figure and were included; the remainder lacked a GDP estimate in the source used (chiefly small territories and countries without recent World Bank national accounts data, e.g., North Korea, Cuba, Eritrea) and were excluded.
Time series: All calendar years 1960–2024 for the United States for which both series report a value. No years were missing; n = 65.


Variables
Outcome (both designs): Life expectancy at birth, in years — the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates at the time of observation stayed constant over its lifetime.
Exposure (both designs): GDP per capita — gross domestic product divided by population. Cross-sectional GDP per capita is expressed in current US dollars; time-series GDP per capita is expressed in constant 2010 US dollars (to remove the effect of US inflation over the 65-year window, which a current-dollar figure would otherwise confound with real income growth).


Data sources and measurement

Bias
Three sources of potential bias are noted. First, the cross-section combines life expectancy from one producer (CIA World Factbook) and GDP per capita from another (World Bank), reported in different years (~2024 and 2023 respectively) and compiled by different aggregator sites; this is a comparability concern rather than a random-error concern, since it could shift the estimated correlation in either direction depending on how each source’s methodology and reference year diverge. Second, both cross-sectional variables, and both time-series variables, come from a single World Bank lineage in the time-series case, reducing (but not eliminating) that specific concern for the within-country design. Third, and most importantly for interpretation: no adjustment was made, in either design, for variables that plausibly affect both life expectancy and income at once (education, disease environment, war, and — specific to the time-series design — the passage of calendar time itself, during which medical technology improved independently of any single country’s income growth). This is addressed further under Limitations.


Study size
Study size was determined by data availability rather than by a power calculation: all countries with matched data in the cross-section (n = 175), and all years with matched data in the US time series (n = 65).


Quantitative variables
GDP per capita was analyzed in two forms in both designs: untransformed (dollars) and natural-log-transformed. The log transform was included because the Preston curve is a well-documented concave relationship — equal dollar increases in income are associated with larger life-expectancy gains at low income than at high income — and a linear (Pearson) correlation on untransformed income will understate the strength of a genuinely monotonic but curved association. Life expectancy was analyzed untransformed (years) in both designs.


Statistical methods
All associations are reported as the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, computed the same way in both designs — the only difference is what the index runs over:
Cross-section (country i = 1…n):
r = Σi(xi − x̄)(yi − ȳ) / √[Σi(xi − x̄)² · Σi(yi − ȳ)²]
Time series (year t = 1…T, single country):
r = Σt(xt − x̄)(yt − ȳ) / √[Σt(xt − x̄)² · Σt(yt − ȳ)²]
No regression model was fit in either design; only the correlation coefficient, its two-sided p-value (against the null of r = 0), and sample size are reported. This choice is deliberate and is returned to in the Discussion.
Why a correlation coefficient is a valid tool here, and where it stops being one. A Pearson correlation is a valid summary of the strength and direction of a linear (or, after transformation, monotonic) association between two variables, and its significance test is valid whenever observations are independent and the usual regularity conditions hold. It becomes an unreliable guide to the underlying relationship in at least three situations relevant here. First, when the association is driven by a third variable that independently moves both x and y — classically, a confounder. Second, when the data are aggregated units rather than the individual-level units the relationship is really about (the ecological fallacy): a correlation between country-level averages can differ in sign or magnitude from the correlation that would be observed within any single country, and vice versa. Third, in time series specifically, when both variables share a common trend — two unrelated series that both rise steadily over decades will correlate strongly even absent any causal link between them, because “time” itself is the omitted third variable. All three concerns are directly relevant to interpreting the results below, and are addressed in the Discussion.
Why life expectancy and GDP per capita are a good pair for illustrating this. The relationship is real, large, well-replicated, and has a plausible direct mechanism (income buys nutrition, sanitation, and medical care) — so it is not a spurious or trivial example. But it is simultaneously a textbook case for every one of the three correlation pitfalls above: countries differ on many confounders correlated with income (education, governance, disease burden); the cross-sectional relationship is explicitly known, from Preston’s own work, to have shifted over historical time in a way that a single correlation coefficient cannot reveal; and the US time series in particular spans a period (1960–2024) of dramatic medical progress that plausibly drove much of the life-expectancy gain independent of income growth. It is, in other words, a relationship where “the correlation is strong” is true and also nowhere near the end of the story.

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis
section: Discussion
text:
Discussion

Key results
Both the cross-sectional and the time-series design show a strong, positive, statistically significant correlation between life expectancy and GDP per capita, and in both designs the relationship strengthens under a log transform of income. Taken at face value, the two designs agree: countries with higher income tend to have higher life expectancy, and the United States’ own life expectancy has risen closely alongside its own income over 65 years.


Limitations
This is a correlational analysis of unadjusted, aggregated national statistics, and its limitations follow directly from the three concerns raised in Methods. No confounders were controlled for, so neither r cannot separate a direct income→health effect from confounding by education, governance, disease environment, or (in the time series) simple calendar time, during which antibiotics, vaccination, and neonatal care advanced independent of any single country’s income growth. The cross-section mixes two data producers observed in different years, a comparability limitation noted above. And a single Pearson r, by construction, reports only the strength of the association at the level analyzed — it says nothing about whether the same relationship (the same slope, the same curve) holds across the two designs, only that a relationship of some strength holds in each. A companion piece in this series (the “Preston curve” post on the Goldin data pattern) shows directly, by plotting the US time path against the cross-sectional curve, that the two need not coincide even when both correlations are strong.


Interpretation
A cautious reading of these results is that income and life expectancy move together, strongly, both across countries and within the United States over time — but a correlation coefficient alone cannot say whether income is doing the causal work, in either design, or how much of each estimate reflects a genuine income effect versus a shared trend or common cause. The very high time-series correlation (r = 0.97 on log income) is exactly the pattern one would also expect to see if life expectancy and income were both simply rising over the same 65 years for largely unrelated reasons (medical technology improving on its own trajectory; income growing on its own) — the correlation coefficient, by design, cannot distinguish these two stories from each other.


Generalizability
The cross-sectional estimate describes the relationship across the specific set of 175 countries included here at one point in time and should not be assumed to describe the relationship within any individual country as it develops; the time-series estimate describes the United States specifically and should not be assumed to generalize to other countries, which may follow a different path (as this series has already shown directly for female labor force participation, where three of four countries with long-run data showed no U-shape at all despite a robust cross-sectional U).

title: Life Expectancy and National Income: A Cross-Sectional and Time-Series Correlation Analysis
section: Conclusion and next steps
text:
Conclusion and next steps
Both designs here return a strong, statistically significant, unadjusted correlation between income and life expectancy, and the log-income version is stronger than the linear one in each case — a first, purely descriptive answer to whether “the correlation holds” across designs. What an unadjusted correlation coefficient cannot deliver is a quantified relationship one could use to predict, compare magnitudes across the two designs on a common scale, or begin separating a shared time trend from a direct association. The next post in this series will fit an unadjusted ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to both the cross-sectional and time-series data, which will add: an explicit slope (years of life expectancy per log-dollar of income) directly comparable between the two designs; an R² describing how much of the variance in life expectancy each design’s income measure accounts for; and residual plots that can start to reveal where the two designs’ relationships diverge, rather than only whether a correlation exists in each. That step remains, deliberately, still unadjusted for confounders — a fully adjusted model is a further step beyond it.

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
text: Data Story  ·  Boston, MA  ·  Weather and Climate

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: One city, two weather stations
text:
One city, two weather stations
A 133-year daily temperature record for any single American city doesn’t come from one continuous source. Boston’s does not either. From 1893 to 1935, the official readings came from a downtown “Boston City” station; since 1936, they’ve come from Boston Logan International Airport, built on filled tidal flats in East Boston. Both feed into the same NOAA-maintained record used here, and splicing stations like this is standard practice in long climate series — it’s the same approach the National Weather Service itself uses to construct Boston’s official climate normals.
It’s also a genuine caveat rather than a footnote. Airport stations tend to sit on open, paved ground surrounded by jet exhaust and less vegetation than a downtown site, which can nudge readings — especially daytime highs — slightly warmer than an old-city location would show for identical weather. The 1936 station change is marked on the chart below; it’s worth keeping in mind when comparing eras on either side of that line.








Annual average of daily high and low temperatures, Boston, MA, 1893–2025. Dotted line marks 1936, when the official record switches from the downtown Boston City station to Boston Logan International Airport. Green line is a trailing 10-year average of the annual mean temperature ((high + low) / 2), smoothing year-to-year noise to show the underlying trend. Click any legend item to isolate that line.



Warmest year on record 2021 Average high 61.8°F, average low 47.3°F


Coldest year on record 1904 Average high 55.1°F, average low 39.3°F


Daytime high, 1893–1902 → 2016–2025 +3.1°F Decade average rose from 57.7°F to 60.9°F


Nighttime low, 1893–1902 → 2016–2025 +4.0°F Decade average rose from 42.1°F to 46.1°F — nights are warming faster than days

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: Nights are warming faster than days
text:
Nights are warming faster than days
The gap between the two lines has narrowed over time, and that’s the more interesting half of the story. If Boston were simply getting a uniformly warmer version of the same climate, the high and low lines would have shifted upward by roughly the same amount. Instead, the average low has risen about four degrees since the 1890s, versus roughly three degrees for the average high.
This isn’t unique to Boston — nighttime lows warming faster than daytime highs is a well-documented pattern across much of the United States, and several forces plausibly contribute: cloud cover and humidity trap outgoing heat overnight, urban and airport development reduces how quickly the ground radiates heat away after sunset, and warming winters mean fewer of the historically frigid, clear, dry nights that used to pull the coldest lows down hard. Because Logan Airport itself has been built up substantially since 1936 — more pavement, more infrastructure, more heat-retaining surface around the immediate station — some of this narrowing could also reflect the station’s own changing surroundings rather than the regional climate alone. Both are almost certainly part of the picture; disentangling exactly how much is beyond what this single-station record can settle.

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: A record increasingly stacked with recent years
text:
A record increasingly stacked with recent years
The chart’s ranking tells its own story. Of the ten warmest years since 1893, eight occurred in 2010 or later: 2021, 2012, 2023, 2010, 2024, 2022, 2020, and 2016. But the list isn’t a clean, monotonic march upward — 1949 and 1953 also crack the top ten, both comfortably warmer than most years around them. Those two mid-century years are a reminder that a single unusually warm year has always been possible in Boston’s climate; what’s changed is the odds. A “top-ten warmest year” used to be a rare, scattered event across the twentieth century. Now it is the typical outcome of any given year in the 2010s and 2020s.

title: How Much Has Boston Warmed? 133 Years of Daily Highs and Lows
section: What a single station can’t tell you
text:
What a single station can’t tell you
This is one station’s daily-average record, and it leaves real gaps. It says nothing about precipitation, snowfall, or storm intensity — a separate and increasingly important part of New England’s changing climate. It says nothing about single-day extremes: a year with a mild average can still contain a record-breaking heat wave or cold snap that this chart smooths away entirely. It reflects one site’s specific microclimate — coastal, low-lying, airport-adjacent — which won’t match temperature trends recorded a few miles inland or at higher elevation. And because the underlying source splices two station records at 1936, some caution is warranted when comparing eras directly across that seam. A natural next post on this thread would push into extremes directly: the frequency of 90°F+ days, or how the length of Boston’s frost-free growing season has changed over the same 133 years.


Sources: Annual average daily high and low temperatures for Boston, Massachusetts, 1893–2025, based on NOAA climate data (Boston City station, 1893–1935; Boston Logan International Airport, GHCND:USW00014739, 1936–2025), as compiled by Extreme Weather Watch.

title: The Camera in Everyone’s Pocket
text: Data Story  ·  IDC  ·  CIPA

title: The Camera in Everyone’s Pocket
section: Two industries, one dataset problem
text:
Two industries, one dataset problem
The camera side of this story is CIPA’s — the same worldwide shipment data used in our earlier post on the DSLR-to-mirrorless transition. The smartphone side comes from IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker, the industry-standard source that most outlets (and Statista’s own smartphone-shipment statistics) ultimately cite. The two trackers don’t share a methodology — IDC counts all Android and iOS manufacturers combined, CIPA counts a defined list of Japanese-headquartered camera brands — but both report worldwide unit shipments to the same rough standard, which is what makes overlaying them meaningful.
2007–2009 smartphone totals are reconstructed estimates (IDC’s own press archive gets sparse before its 2010–2011 releases), interpolated between known points: Apple’s own reported 3.3 million iPhones in 2007, RIM’s roughly 20% share of a 175-million-unit market in 2009, and Nokia’s continued Symbian dominance through the period. 2010 onward are IDC’s own published totals, cited repeatedly across its press releases. Compact camera figures are CIPA’s, identical to the previous post.








Worldwide unit shipments, log scale (necessary since the two lines span three orders of magnitude by the end of the period). Smartphone totals: IDC Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker (2007–2009 estimated, see note above). Compact/fixed-lens camera totals: CIPA.



2007: smartphones vs. compacts 122M vs. 92M Smartphones — across all makers, not just Apple — already outshipped dedicated compacts the year the iPhone launched


2016: smartphone peak 1.47B Same year CIPA’s compact shipments fell below 13 million — an 116-to-1 ratio


2025 ratio 516-to-1 1.26 billion smartphones shipped for every 2.4 million compact cameras


Compact camera decline, 2010–2023 −98.4% 108.6 million units (2010) to 1.7 million (2023), CIPA’s trough year

title: The Camera in Everyone’s Pocket
section: The pioneer that got left behind
text:
The pioneer that got left behind
BlackBerry’s own trajectory is a case study within the case study. RIM held its cameras back for years on principle — the BlackBerry 7230 (2003) had Bluetooth and a color screen but no camera; corporate IT departments and government buildings were actively hostile to camera phones at the time, and RIM’s whole business was selling into those buildings. The Pearl broke with that policy in 2006, and it worked: RIM’s shipments roughly tripled over the next four years, peaking around 2011. Then BlackBerry OS’s browser, app ecosystem, and touchscreen kept losing to iOS and Android, the camera-first feature that once differentiated the Pearl became table stakes on every phone, and BlackBerry’s hardware shipments collapsed even faster than they’d grown.





BlackBerry (RIM) worldwide smartphone shipments, calendar-year estimates reconstructed from RIM/BlackBerry quarterly and fiscal-year filings (SEC Forms 6-K and 40-F) and contemporaneous market-share reporting; RIM’s fiscal year ran March–February, so calendar-year figures are approximate. Shipments fell below 1 million annually by 2016, after which BlackBerry-branded phones were made under license by TCL rather than by BlackBerry itself.



First BlackBerry with a camera 2006 BlackBerry Pearl 8100, 1.3 MP — RIM had avoided cameras until then for enterprise-security reasons


BlackBerry peak shipments ~51M Calendar 2011, roughly five years after adding a camera


Fiscal 2012 → fiscal 2013 −42.7% Shipments fell from ~49.0M to ~28.1M in a single fiscal year, per RIM’s own 40-F filing


Global smartphone share, Q1 2011 → 2013 13.6% → <3% BlackBerry’s collapse in relative terms was even faster than in absolute units

title: The Camera in Everyone’s Pocket
section: The feature that won wasn’t the camera
text:
The feature that won wasn’t the camera
It’s tempting to read this as “camera phones killed cameras,” and directionally that’s right — but BlackBerry’s own arc shows the camera alone was never the differentiator. RIM added a perfectly serviceable camera in 2006 and gained share for years afterward; it lost that share to companies that paired a camera with instant sharing, an app ecosystem, and a touchscreen built around photos and video rather than email. The compact camera didn’t lose to “a camera in a phone” — it lost to a phone where the camera was one part of a always-with-you, always-connected package that no dedicated camera, however good the sensor, could match. Which is also, per the previous post, exactly the gap mirrorless cameras and revived point-and-shoots are now trying to compete on different terms altogether: image quality and a deliberate, single-purpose object, rather than convenience.

Sources: International Data Corporation (IDC), Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker, as reported in IDC press releases and widely re-cited by Statista, GSMArena, PhoneArena, and InformationWeek; 2007–2009 figures are estimated (see methodology note above). Camera & Imaging Products Association (CIPA), worldwide digital still camera shipment statistics, as used in the companion post on this site. BlackBerry/RIM shipment figures are reconstructed from Research In Motion/BlackBerry SEC filings (Forms 6-K, 40-F) and contemporaneous market-share reporting from Statista and businesstats.com.

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
text: Data Story  ·  CIPA  ·  Camera & Imaging Products Association

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
section: Finding a real time series
text:
Finding a real time series
CIPA, the Japanese trade association whose members include Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, Panasonic, and Olympus/OM Digital, has published monthly worldwide shipment data since the 1990s and is the industry-standard source everyone from Statista to DPReview ultimately cites. The association’s own historical PDF archive isn’t set up for scraping, so the series below is reconstructed from CIPA’s published monthly and annual releases as reported by CIPA itself and cross-checked against PetaPixel, DPReview, Nikon Rumors, and Statista, rather than pulled from a single downloadable file.
2007 is where a clean, comparable annual series becomes possible: that’s the first year CIPA’s own releases split shipments into “built-in lens” (compact) and “interchangeable lens” (DSLR-and-later-mirrorless) totals, and it’s also the year worldwide shipments first broke 100 million units. Before 2007, comparable digital-era data exists (roughly 5 million units shipped in 1995, the digital camera’s standing start) but isn’t broken out by camera type, so it’s mentioned qualitatively rather than charted.
Splitting that “interchangeable lens” total into DSLR and mirrorless separately is a harder problem, because CIPA didn’t report the two as distinct categories in its own headline releases until well into the format’s life. Mirrorless launched in September 2008 (Panasonic’s Lumix G1) and was a rounding error for years afterward, so 2007–2011 below shows essentially all interchangeable-lens shipments as DSLR. From 2012 the mirrorless share is interpolated against known product milestones — Sony’s a7 brought full-frame mirrorless in 2013; Nikon and Canon didn’t commit to full-frame mirrorless systems of their own until 2018 — anchored to three points CIPA itself has published: mirrorless overtook DSLR within the interchangeable-lens category for the first time in 2020 (51.5%), reached 68.7% by 2022, and 80.5% by 2023. 2024 and 2025 are CIPA’s own reported figures. The interpolated stretch (2012–2019, and 2021) is flagged in the chart note below; treat it as the shape of the transition rather than exact annual counts.








Worldwide shipments by CIPA member companies, log scale (necessary since compact shipments outnumbered interchangeable-lens cameras 10-to-1 in the 2000s, then the ranking flipped). Total shown as a thin dashed line for reference — click any legend item to isolate or hide it. 2007–2011 and 2020/2022/2023/2024/2025 DSLR and mirrorless figures are CIPA’s own reported numbers; 2012–2019 and 2021 are interpolated between those points against known product-launch dates (see note above) and shouldn’t be read as exact annual counts.



2010 peak 121.5M Highest annual shipment total CIPA has recorded


2023 trough 7.7M 93.6% below the 2010 peak — the smartphone-driven collapse


2025 shipments 9.4M Second consecutive annual increase — first back-to-back growth since the mid-2000s


Growth off the trough +22.3% 2023 → 2025, though still a sliver of the 2010 peak

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
section: The format war: who won the shrinking pie
text:
The format war: who won the shrinking pie
The total collapsed, but the mix inside it changed even more dramatically. In 2010, compact point-and-shoots — the cameras smartphones killed first — still accounted for 109 million of the 121.5 million units shipped, with DSLRs and the still-new mirrorless format (Panasonic’s Lumix G1, the first mirrorless model, had shipped roughly two years earlier) making up the remaining 12.5 million between them. By 2025, the compact category had shrunk to 2.4 million units but mirrorless had grown into the dominant force in the industry at 6.3 million units, while DSLRs — which Canon and Nikon have largely stopped developing — had fallen to just 691,000, kept alive mainly by Pentax and a market for cheap used bodies.





2010: CIPA reported compact and interchangeable-lens shipments as two categories; mirrorless was under 1% of the 12.5M interchangeable-lens total that year and isn’t broken out separately. 2025: DSLR, mirrorless, and compact are each reported individually by CIPA.



Mirrorless share, 2025 66.9% Up from a rounding error in 2010; overtook compacts as the top category in 2022


DSLR share, 2025 7.3% 691,000 units, down from ~998,000 in 2024 — Canon and Nikon have largely exited the format


Compact shipments, 2025 +29.6% 2.4M units, the fastest-growing category — a “digicam” revival led by younger buyers


Avg. export value per body $282 vs $711 DSLR vs. mirrorless, 2025 — most remaining DSLR volume is low-end inventory, not pro gear

title: Cameras After the Smartphone
section: Two different recoveries, one chart
text:
Two different recoveries, one chart
The 2024–2025 uptick isn’t one story but two. At the top of the market, mirrorless bodies keep getting more expensive and more capable, and buyers — increasingly professionals and serious enthusiasts rather than casual shooters — keep paying for them; shipment value has grown faster than unit volume for several years running. At the bottom, a cohort too young to have owned a point-and-shoot the first time around has been driving demand for compact cameras like the Fujifilm X100 series and screen-free novelties like the Camp Snap, treating a dedicated camera as a deliberate alternative to a phone rather than a worse version of one. Both trends show up as growth in the same chart, but they’re selling to different customers for different reasons — which is presumably why CIPA’s own 2026 shipment forecasts still describe a wide range (6.3–7.4 million interchangeable-lens bodies) rather than a confident single number.

Sources: Camera & Imaging Products Association (CIPA), worldwide monthly and annual digital still camera shipment statistics, as reported by CIPA and independently cited by PetaPixel, DPReview, Digital Camera World, Fstoppers, and Statista. 2025 figures reflect CIPA’s full-year release (February 2026); 2026 references are CIPA’s preliminary/forecast data as of mid-2026. The 2010 compact/interchangeable-lens split is drawn from CIPA’s own reported totals for that year.

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
text: Data Story  ·  United States  ·  Wages and Prices

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
section: Picking the right yardsticks
text:
Picking the right yardsticks
Before plotting anything, two questions needed answers: whose wages, and whose prices?
For wages, the cleanest candidate would be something like median household income — except the Census Bureau didn’t start publishing that until 1947. Nominal GDP per capita reaches back further, but it blends labor income with capital income and divides by total population rather than hours worked, so it answers “how rich is the country,” not “how far does an hour of work go.” The series economic historians actually use for this comparison is average hourly earnings of production workers in manufacturing. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has published it continuously since 1939; the NBER’s Macrohistory Database and the economic-history site MeasuringWorth extend it back to 1900 by linking two earlier academic series. It’s the standard choice for a century-long view, for the simple reason that nothing else covers the period as consistently.
That choice comes with a real caveat. It’s a manufacturing, blue-collar measure in an economy that has moved overwhelmingly into services, and it counts cash wages only — leaving out the employer-paid health insurance and retirement contributions that have grown from negligible to a large share of total compensation since the 1960s. Total compensation almost certainly grew faster than the cash-wage line below, especially in recent decades; this chart is deliberately the more conservative, more consistently measured slice of the story.
For prices, the Consumer Price Index is the more straightforward call: it’s the standard cost-of-living yardstick, built to track what a household actually spends on housing, food, transportation, and the like. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis publishes a continuous CPI series back to 1800, splicing the official BLS index (1913–present) onto three earlier historical estimates the BLS itself compiled for its Handbook of Labor Statistics.








Index, 1900 = 100, log scale (a straight line on this scale means a constant growth rate, which makes it possible to compare series growing at very different speeds on one axis). Dotted lines mark 1929 (onset of the Depression) and 1973, the year economists most often cite as the start of the long real-wage slowdown. Click any legend item to isolate that line. Wage series splices five underlying sources; Consumer Price Index splices four. See methodology and sources below.



Nominal wage growth, 1900–2025 194× 15.2¢/hr in 1900 → $29.51/hr in 2025, average factory pay


Price level growth, 1900–2025 38.7× What $1.00 bought in 1900 costs $38.70 today


Real (purchasing-power) wage growth 5.0× An hour of factory work buys 5× what it did in 1900, after inflation


Real wages, 1973 → 2025 −0.5% Essentially flat for half a century, despite nominal pay rising 7× further

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
section: Three eras of pay
text:
Three eras of pay
The 126-year run breaks into three distinct phases, and the breakpoints aren’t subtle.
1900–1929. Factory wages roughly quadrupled in nominal terms, but World War I inflation took a large bite out of the gain. Real purchasing power still rose by close to 80% over these three decades — a genuine, if uneven, improvement.
The Depression and the war, 1930–1945. Nominal wages fell sharply in the early 1930s, but prices fell even faster, so real wages held up better than the headlines from the period suggest, before climbing again under wartime labor demand and the wage and price controls of the early 1940s.
The postwar golden age, 1946–1973. This is where the real wage line is steepest. Driven by strong productivity growth, high union density in manufacturing, and a tight postwar labor market, real factory pay nearly tripled again between the end of the war and 1973 — the single best sustained stretch in the dataset.
Since 1973. The real wage index has barely moved: 504 in 1973, 502 in 2025. Nominal wages and consumer prices have both continued climbing — nominal pay is up more than sevenfold since 1973 alone — but almost none of that nominal gain has translated into added purchasing power for this particular measure of pay. Economists point to several plausible, overlapping explanations for the slowdown: the shrinking share of the workforce employed in manufacturing itself, declining private-sector union membership, the erosion of the real value of the minimum wage, a shift in total compensation toward non-wage benefits that this wage-only measure doesn’t capture, and the effects of automation and global trade competition on demand for manufacturing labor specifically. There’s no single, settled answer in the research, and the relative weight of each factor remains actively debated.

title: Wages vs. Prices: A Century of American Pay
section: What this measure can’t tell you
text:
What this measure can’t tell you
A national average hides as much as it reveals. It says nothing about how pay has diverged by region, industry, education, race, or gender over the same period, and it says nothing about the well-documented widening gap between average and median pay since the 1980s — a separate and important part of the inequality story that a single average wage line cannot show. It is also, deliberately, a manufacturing-sector measure in an economy where manufacturing’s employment share has fallen for decades; a similar exercise using service-sector or all-private-sector pay (available only from 1964 onward) would likely tell a somewhat different recent story. And because it tracks cash wages only, it understates how total compensation — wages plus benefits — has grown, particularly since employer-sponsored health insurance became widespread. Future posts on this site could push further into any of these threads: a sectoral breakdown, a look at the minimum wage specifically, or a comparison against productivity growth.


Sources: Wages — U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Average Hourly Earnings of Production and Nonsupervisory Employees, Manufacturing (series CES3000000008), 1939–2025; National Bureau of Economic Research Macrohistory Database, series a08050a (Paul H. Douglas, Real Wages in the United States, 1890–1926) for 1900–1919 and series a08050b (National Industrial Conference Board, Wages, Hours, and Employment in the United States: 1914–1936) for 1920–1933; 1934–1938 linearly interpolated between these two series due to a gap in consistent annual reporting during the NIRA/early-FLSA transition. Prices — Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, Consumer Price Index, 1800– (splicing BLS historical cost-of-living estimates for 1900–1912 with the official Consumer Price Index, 1913–2025).

title: Fear Gauges and Headlines
text: Machine Learning for Social Science  ·  Boston, MA

title: Fear Gauges and Headlines
section: Example 1: Market fear and the news, over time
text:
Example 1: Market fear and the news, over time
The variables. The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) is the options market’s 30-day forward-looking measure of expected S&P 500 volatility — Wall Street’s “fear gauge.” The San Francisco Fed Daily News Sentiment Index is a daily sentiment score built by scoring economics-related articles across 16 major U.S. newspapers, smoothed into a continuous time series back to 1980. Both are daily, both are United States–based, and both are free to download.
Sourcing. VIX: CBOE Volatility Index, retrieved from FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), series VIXCLS. News sentiment: Shapiro, Sudhof & Wilson (2020), Daily News Sentiment Index, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. The overlap between the two series runs from January 3, 2000 to September 11, 2026 — 6,747 trading days.

Descriptive statistics

sd 8.27 · range 9.14–82.69

right-skewed, as fear gauges tend to be

The chart
Monthly averages of both series, January 2000–September 2026:






Correlation



Pearson r · levels


−0.61


p < 0.001, n = 6,747 daily obs.




Pearson r · daily changes


0.005


p = 0.66 — not distinguishable from zero



The levels of VIX and news sentiment are strongly negatively correlated (r = −0.61): when the market is fearful, the news is gloomier, and vice versa. That is the correlation most people mean when they say “the market and the news move together.” But when the same two series are converted to day-over-day changes — did VIX and sentiment move together from one day to the next — the correlation collapses to essentially zero. That gap is itself the lesson: a strong correlation in levels can come almost entirely from both series drifting through the same multi-year regimes (calm 2000s, the 2008 crisis, COVID, etc.), not from any tight day-to-day linkage between newsroom tone and options pricing.

title: Fear Gauges and Headlines
section: Example 2: Policy uncertainty and market volatility, across countries
text:
Example 2: Policy uncertainty and market volatility, across countries
The variables. Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU), the Baker-Bloom-Davis index built from the frequency of policy-uncertainty language in national newspapers, one score per country per month. Paired against each country’s equity volatility for the same month — the VIX-style implied-volatility reading where a clean monthly figure was obtainable.

p = 0.40 — a moderate rank relationship, not significant



With only four countries, this correlation carries almost no statistical weight on its own (n = 4 leaves just two degrees of freedom) — it is included to show the mechanics of a cross-sectional correlation, not to make a claim about the world. Worth noticing anyway: Germany has by far the highest EPU reading (roughly three times the next-highest country) but a middling volatility reading, which alone is enough to flatten the linear (Pearson) relationship even though the rank (Spearman) relationship still points positive.

title: Fear Gauges and Headlines
section: Why the correlation might not mean what it looks like
text:
Why the correlation might not mean what it looks like
In the time-series example, the headline result (r = −0.61 in levels, r ≈ 0 in changes) points to a specific third factor: the macroeconomic regime. VIX and news sentiment both drift with the business cycle — both were low and calm for most of the mid-2000s, both moved sharply in 2008 and again in 2020 — so a big share of their correlation in levels is really both series independently tracking the same underlying economic conditions, rather than one driving the other day to day. The fact that the correlation nearly disappears in first differences is the tell.
In the cross-country example, the plausible third factor is different: EPU counts newspaper mentions of policy uncertainty, while an implied-volatility index prices option-market risk. A country can generate a great deal of uncertainty-flavored news coverage — coalition politics, fiscal debates, regulatory fights — without that translating into elevated pricing of equity risk, and Germany in July 2026 looks like exactly that case. The two variables are related in principle (both are trying to measure “uncertainty”) but are constructed from different underlying processes (text mentions vs. option prices), which is enough to decouple them country by country.
